title: Bactrim and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Sulfamethoxazole?
excerpt: Can you drink on Bactrim? The real risks of mixing sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim with alcohol: rare flushing reactions, folate, low blood sugar, and how long to wait.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Bactrim? The real risks: rare flushing reactions, low folate, low blood sugar, liver strain, and how long to wait after your last dose.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Bactrim (sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim) is not one of the antibiotics with a famous, dangerous alcohol reaction. That reputation belongs to metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole. The US prescribing information for Bactrim does not list alcohol as a contraindication, and many pharmacists will tell you that a single drink is unlikely to cause a crisis. But "no strict ban" is not the same as "no problem." There are a handful of published case reports of a disulfiram-like reaction (sudden flushing, a pounding heart, headache, and nausea, like the reaction to the alcohol-aversion drug Antabuse) in people who drank on Bactrim, both the drug and alcohol can lower your folate and your blood sugar, both can be hard on the liver, and both can upset your stomach. On top of that, alcohol works against the reason you're taking the drug in the first place: getting over an infection. The safest plan is to skip alcohol until you've finished the course and given it a couple of days to clear, and to ask your prescriber if you have any of the risk factors below.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink heavily or binge while on Bactrim. If you choose to have a drink, keep it to one, have it with food, drink plenty of water, and stop if you feel flushed, dizzy, shaky, or sick. Never skip or delay a dose so you can drink. Wait about 48 to 72 hours after your last dose before drinking normally again. If you drink most days, have diabetes, liver or kidney problems, are older, or are underweight, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking at all on this drug.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and why you were prescribed Bactrim. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on Bactrim if** you drink alcohol most days, have liver or kidney disease, have diabetes or take diabetes pills such as glipizide or glyburide, take a blood thinner such as warfarin, take methotrexate or seizure medicine, are pregnant, or have been told you have low folate. **Get urgent care (call 911 in an emergency) if** you develop a spreading rash, blisters, peeling skin or mouth sores, yellow skin or eyes, severe stomach pain, trouble breathing, a racing heart with chest pain, or signs of very low blood sugar such as confusion, shaking, and sweating that don't improve after eating.

## What Bactrim Is and How It Works

Bactrim is a brand name for a two-drug combination: **sulfamethoxazole** (a sulfa antibiotic) and **trimethoprim**. You may also see it called Septra, Bactrim DS, SMX-TMP, or co-trimoxazole. The "DS" stands for double strength, which is 800 mg of sulfamethoxazole and 160 mg of trimethoprim in one tablet. Doctors commonly prescribe it for urinary tract infections, some skin infections including certain MRSA infections, traveler's diarrhea, some ear and respiratory infections, and for preventing a type of pneumonia in people with weakened immune systems.

The two drugs work as a team by blocking how bacteria make **folate** (folic acid), a B vitamin that all cells need to build DNA. Sulfamethoxazole blocks an earlier step, and trimethoprim blocks a later one. Bacteria have to make their own folate, so cutting off two steps in the same assembly line hits them hard.

Human cells get folate from food rather than making it, so the drug is much gentler on us than on bacteria. But trimethoprim does have some effect on the human version of the enzyme it targets, and that's one of the reasons alcohol comes up. Hold onto that idea, because folate is one of the threads that connects Bactrim and drinking.

## Can You Drink Alcohol on Bactrim?

Here's what's known, without the scare tactics or the false reassurance.

**There is no official ban.** The US labeling for sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim does not list alcohol as a contraindication, and it is not in the same category as metronidazole, where drinking can trigger a well-documented reaction. If you had one glass of wine at dinner before realizing you were on an antibiotic, the most likely outcome is nothing at all.

**But the label does mention drinkers.** The prescribing information warns that people who may already be low in folate, and it specifically lists chronic alcohol use alongside older age, malnutrition, malabsorption, and seizure medicines, are at greater risk of folate-related side effects. So alcohol is not invisible to the drug's own safety warnings.

**And the two overlap in side effects.** Bactrim commonly causes nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. Alcohol does too. Bactrim can, rarely, injure the liver and lower blood sugar. Alcohol can do both as well. Taking two things that push in the same direction makes it more likely that you'll feel the push.

So the practical answer for most people is this: an occasional single drink is unlikely to be dangerous for a healthy adult, but it's a poor idea while you're sick, it can make you feel worse, and there are specific groups for whom it's a real risk. Most doctors and pharmacists simply recommend avoiding alcohol until the course is done.

## The "Disulfiram-Like" Reaction: Myth or Real?

You'll find two camps online. One says Bactrim and alcohol cause a violent reaction and must never be mixed. The other says the whole antibiotics-and-alcohol warning is a myth. The truth sits in between.

### What a disulfiram-like reaction is

Disulfiram (Antabuse) is a drug that blocks the enzyme that clears **acetaldehyde**, the toxic substance your body makes when it first breaks down alcohol. When acetaldehyde builds up, you get a strong, unpleasant reaction: facial flushing, a pounding or racing heart, a throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, and sometimes a drop in blood pressure. Any drug that causes a similar effect with alcohol gets called "disulfiram-like."

### Where Bactrim fits

For Bactrim, the evidence is a small number of published case reports describing people who developed this kind of flushing and racing-heart reaction after drinking while on sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Case reports are real observations, but they're individual stories. They show that something *can* happen; they don't tell you how often it happens or prove the drug was the cause. There is no good evidence that this reaction is common with Bactrim, and it is not considered a routine interaction the way it is with metronidazole.

What this means in practice:

- **It's uncommon, not impossible.** Most people who have a drink on Bactrim won't get this reaction.
- **You can't predict who will.** If it happens, it's usually within minutes to an hour of drinking.
- **If it happens, stop drinking.** Sit or lie down, drink water, and let it pass. If you have chest pain, fainting, severe vomiting, or trouble breathing, get emergency care.

If the reaction you're worried about sounds familiar because your face turns red with any drink, that may be the separate, genetic version of the same acetaldehyde buildup. Our guide to [Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains how that works.

### The bigger myth

The broader belief that *all* antibiotics react badly with alcohol is mostly a myth. Many common antibiotics, like amoxicillin, have no direct chemical interaction with a drink. A few, though, really do: metronidazole and tinidazole are the clearest examples, and others have specific issues. Our overview of [antibiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) sorts the real interactions from the folklore, and our guide to [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) covers the one that actually deserves the strict "no alcohol" rule. Bactrim sits in the middle: no strict ban, but more reasons for caution than amoxicillin.

## Folate: The Quiet Interaction

This is the interaction that gets the least attention online but has the clearest basis in the drug's own label.

Both sides of the equation work against your folate:

- **Bactrim's trimethoprim** interferes with the enzyme that turns folate into its active form. In healthy people with good folate stores, a short course rarely causes trouble.
- **Regular drinking lowers folate.** Heavy alcohol use reduces how much folate you absorb from food, increases how much you lose in urine, and often comes with a diet that's low in folate to begin with. Low folate is common in people who drink heavily.

When someone who's already low in folate takes Bactrim, the risk of folate-related problems goes up. These can include changes in blood cell counts, such as a type of anemia where red blood cells come out too large, and low white cell or platelet counts. This is the reason the label lists chronic alcohol use as a risk factor and the reason doctors sometimes order blood tests or add folic acid for people on longer courses.

For a social drinker on a five- to fourteen-day course for a UTI, this is unlikely to be an issue. For someone who drinks most days, or is on Bactrim for weeks or months, it's worth mentioning to the prescriber.

## Low Blood Sugar: A Double Hit

This is the risk most people have never heard of, and it's the one that matters most if you have diabetes.

**Bactrim can lower blood sugar.** Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is a known but uncommon side effect. The label notes it is rare in people without diabetes and is more likely in people with kidney or liver problems, people who are malnourished, and people on high doses. Bactrim also slows the breakdown of some diabetes pills, particularly sulfonylureas like glipizide and glyburide, which can push blood sugar down further.

**Alcohol lowers blood sugar too.** When your liver is busy processing alcohol, it puts less effort into making new glucose. That's why drinking without eating, or drinking late and then sleeping, can leave blood sugar low by the morning. People who take insulin or sulfonylureas are especially vulnerable.

Put the two together and you have two separate pressures pushing blood sugar in the same direction. For most healthy people, a single drink with a meal won't tip them into a problem. For someone with diabetes on glipizide who has a few drinks on an empty stomach, it's a real risk.

**Signs of low blood sugar include:** shakiness, sweating, a racing heart, hunger, irritability, confusion, blurred vision, and in severe cases seizures or passing out. Many of these overlap with a hangover or with a disulfiram-like reaction, which is part of the danger: people dismiss them. If you have diabetes, check your sugar rather than guessing, eat something with carbohydrates, and get help if it doesn't improve. Our [alcohol and blood sugar guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) explains more about how drinking affects glucose.

## The Liver, the Kidneys, and Hydration

### Liver

Serious liver injury from Bactrim is rare, but the label does list it, ranging from raised liver enzymes to a form of jaundice caused by blocked bile flow and, very rarely, severe liver failure. Alcohol is processed by the liver and, in heavy amounts, damages it. There's no good evidence that a drink or two in a healthy person meaningfully raises the risk of Bactrim liver injury. But if you already have liver disease, fatty liver, or raised liver enzymes, or you drink heavily, the overlap is worth taking seriously. Yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, or pain under the right ribs while on Bactrim needs prompt medical attention regardless of whether you've been drinking.

### Kidneys and fluids

The Bactrim label tells patients to drink enough fluid to help prevent crystals forming in the urine, which is a known issue with sulfa drugs. Trimethoprim can also raise potassium levels, especially in older people and people with kidney problems. Alcohol makes you pee more and can leave you dehydrated, which works against that fluid advice. If you do drink, match it with water. If you're getting little urine, dark urine, or pain in your side, call your doctor.

## Side Effects That Get Worse Together

Even without a dramatic reaction, alcohol and Bactrim can stack up in ways that make the next day miserable.

| Effect | From Bactrim | From alcohol | Combined |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nausea and vomiting | Common side effect | Common, especially the next day | More likely to feel sick and struggle to keep the pills down |
| Loss of appetite | Common side effect | Common the morning after | Low food intake raises low-blood-sugar and folate risk |
| Dizziness and headache | Reported side effects | Common | Harder to tell what's causing what |
| Dehydration | The label advises plenty of fluid | Alcohol increases urine output | Works against the fluid advice |
| Sun sensitivity | Can make skin burn more easily | No direct effect, but drinking outdoors means more sun time | Easier to burn at a beach or patio |
| Rash | Rash is the most common reason to stop the drug | Flushing can look similar | Can make an early drug rash easier to miss |

That last row is important. A skin rash is one of the more common Bactrim side effects, and in rare cases it can be the first sign of a severe reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Don't write off a new rash as "just from drinking." Call your prescriber about any new rash on Bactrim, and get emergency care if it blisters, peels, spreads fast, or comes with mouth sores, eye pain, or fever.

If nausea is the main problem, our guide to [hangover nausea relief](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has practical tips that also apply when an antibiotic is part of the cause.

## Will Alcohol Stop Bactrim From Working?

Alcohol doesn't chemically switch off sulfamethoxazole or trimethoprim, and there's no good evidence that a single drink makes the antibiotic itself less effective. But alcohol can still get in the way of recovery in a few indirect ways:

- **It can make you miss doses.** Bactrim is usually taken twice a day, about 12 hours apart. A late night is the easiest way to forget the evening dose or sleep through the morning one. Steady levels matter for clearing an infection.
- **Vomiting can lose a dose.** If you throw up soon after taking a tablet, you may not have absorbed it. Ask a pharmacist what to do rather than doubling up.
- **It dampens your immune response.** Heavy drinking is linked with weaker immune defenses. You want your body's own defenses working alongside the antibiotic.
- **It worsens sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep, and rest is part of recovering from an infection.
- **It can irritate the bladder.** If you're on Bactrim for a UTI, alcohol can aggravate bladder irritation and make urgency and burning feel worse.

So while the "alcohol cancels out your antibiotic" idea isn't accurate as a chemical claim, drinking can still mean a slower or rougher recovery.

## Other Medicines That Raise the Stakes

Bactrim interacts with several other medicines, and some of those interactions get worse with alcohol. Tell your prescriber or pharmacist about everything you take, but in particular:

- **Warfarin.** Bactrim can increase warfarin's effect and raise bleeding risk. Alcohol can also affect warfarin. This combination needs close monitoring.
- **Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride).** As above, a higher risk of low blood sugar, which alcohol adds to.
- **Methotrexate.** Bactrim can raise methotrexate levels and both affect folate. Alcohol is also generally discouraged with methotrexate because of liver risk.
- **Phenytoin and some other seizure medicines.** Bactrim can raise phenytoin levels, and seizure medicines can lower folate.
- **ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, and potassium supplements.** Combined with trimethoprim, these can push potassium too high, especially with kidney problems.

For a broader look at how common medications interact with alcohol and with supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## How Long After Bactrim Can You Drink?

Both sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim have a half-life of roughly 10 hours in people with normal kidney function. A half-life is the time it takes for the amount in your blood to drop by half. A common rule of thumb is that a drug is mostly cleared after about five half-lives, which for Bactrim works out to roughly two days. In people with reduced kidney function, it can take longer.

That's where the common advice comes from:

- **Wait about 48 to 72 hours after your last dose** before drinking normally again.
- **Finish the whole course first.** Don't stop early because you feel better and want to go out. Stopping early raises the chance the infection comes back.
- **Make sure you actually feel better.** If you're still sick after the course, that's a reason to call your doctor, not to celebrate.
- **Start light.** Your stomach may still be sensitive for a day or two after finishing an antibiotic.

If your doctor has given you different advice based on your situation, follow theirs.

## Can You Drink the Night Before Starting Bactrim?

If you've had a drink or two and then get a prescription, you don't need to delay starting the antibiotic. Treating the infection on time matters more. Start the course as prescribed, drink water, eat something, and avoid further alcohol. If you had a heavy night, mention it to the pharmacist, who can tell you whether anything about your situation calls for extra caution.

## Who Should Avoid Alcohol on Bactrim Entirely

The risk from mixing is concentrated in specific groups. You should talk to your doctor or pharmacist before having any alcohol on Bactrim if you:

- **Drink most days or binge regularly.** You're more likely to be low in folate and to have liver strain.
- **Have diabetes**, especially if you take insulin or sulfonylureas.
- **Have liver disease or kidney disease**, or have been told your liver enzymes or kidney numbers are off.
- **Are older**, since the label lists older age as a risk factor for several serious side effects.
- **Are underweight, not eating well, or have trouble absorbing food.**
- **Take warfarin, methotrexate, phenytoin, or potassium-raising medicines.**
- **Have HIV or a weakened immune system.** People in this group are more prone to Bactrim side effects and are sometimes on long-term courses.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Alcohol isn't advised in pregnancy in any case, and Bactrim use in pregnancy is a decision for your doctor.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who take Bactrim, with or without an occasional drink, have no serious problems. But a few symptoms should never be brushed off as a hangover.

**Get emergency care (call 911) for:**

- A rash that blisters, peels, or spreads quickly, especially with fever, mouth or eye sores
- Swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing
- Chest pain, fainting, or a racing heart that doesn't settle
- Confusion, seizures, or severe shakiness that doesn't improve after eating sugar

**Call your doctor promptly for:**

- Any new rash
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pale stools
- Unusual bruising or bleeding, sore throat with fever, or unusual paleness or tiredness
- Very little urine, or pain in your side
- Severe or bloody diarrhea, during or even weeks after the course
- Muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of high potassium

If you think you've had a disulfiram-like reaction (sudden flushing, pounding heart, nausea within an hour of a drink), stop drinking and let your prescriber know, so it's on your record.

## How Bactrim Compares With Other Antibiotics

It can help to see where Bactrim sits among the antibiotics people most often ask about.

- **Metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole:** The strictest rule. Avoid alcohol during the course and for a period after, as the label advises. See our [metronidazole guide](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol).
- **Bactrim:** No official ban, but folate, blood sugar, liver, and side-effect overlap, plus occasional case reports of a flushing reaction. Avoid alcohol if you can, especially in the risk groups above.
- **Doxycycline:** Regular heavy drinking may speed up its breakdown. Our [doxycycline and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol) has the details.
- **Amoxicillin:** No direct interaction. The concerns are about recovery and side effects. See our [amoxicillin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol).

## Looking After Yourself After the Course

Once you've finished your Bactrim and given it a couple of days, drinking sensibly is mostly about the same habits that help anyone feel better the next day: eat before and while drinking, alternate with water, pace yourself, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use supplements. Here's an honest view:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It does **not** make it safe to drink on Bactrim, and there's no good evidence that it prevents a disulfiram-like reaction or protects against drug side effects. Its interactions with prescription medicines haven't been well studied, so don't add it while you're on an antibiotic without checking with a pharmacist. If you want to try it for normal social drinking after your course is done, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.
- **Folate-rich food** (leafy greens, beans, lentils, citrus) is a sensible habit if you drink regularly, whether or not you've taken Bactrim. If you think you may be low, ask your doctor about a blood test rather than guessing.

No supplement changes the advice above. While you're on Bactrim, the safest choice is to skip the drink.

## The Bottom Line

- Bactrim does not have an official alcohol ban, and it isn't in the same class as metronidazole.
- A small number of case reports describe a flushing, racing-heart reaction with alcohol. It's uncommon, but it can happen.
- The clearer risks are overlapping effects on **folate, blood sugar, the liver, hydration, and the stomach**, which matter most for regular drinkers, people with diabetes, older adults, and people with liver or kidney problems.
- Alcohol doesn't chemically cancel the antibiotic, but it can lead to missed doses, worse side effects, and slower recovery.
- The safest plan is to avoid alcohol during the course and for about 48 to 72 hours after the last dose. If you're in a higher-risk group, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Bactrim?**

There's no official ban, and an occasional single drink is unlikely to be dangerous for a healthy adult. But alcohol and Bactrim share several side effects, both can lower folate and blood sugar, and there are rare case reports of a flushing, racing-heart reaction. Most doctors and pharmacists recommend avoiding alcohol until you've finished the course. If you drink most days, have diabetes, or have liver or kidney problems, talk to your doctor before drinking at all.

**Is the Bactrim and alcohol warning a myth?**

Partly. The idea that Bactrim causes a guaranteed violent reaction like metronidazole is not accurate. But it's also not true that there's nothing to worry about. A small number of case reports describe a disulfiram-like reaction, and the drug's label lists chronic alcohol use as a risk factor for folate-related side effects. The honest answer is that mixing them is usually not an emergency but is still best avoided.

**How long after taking Bactrim can I drink alcohol?**

A common recommendation is to wait about 48 to 72 hours after your last dose. Both drugs in Bactrim have a half-life of roughly 10 hours in people with normal kidney function, so they are mostly cleared after about two days. Finish the whole course first, make sure your infection has actually cleared, and follow your doctor's advice if it differs.

**What happens if you drink on Bactrim?**

Most people notice nothing beyond feeling a bit worse, since both can cause nausea, headache, and dizziness. Some people may get more stomach upset or low blood sugar, especially if they haven't eaten. Rarely, people have reported a reaction with flushing, a pounding heart, headache, and nausea soon after drinking. If that happens, stop drinking, rest, and drink water, and get emergency care for chest pain, fainting, or trouble breathing.

**Can Bactrim and alcohol cause low blood sugar?**

Yes, both can. Bactrim can rarely cause low blood sugar and can increase the effect of some diabetes pills like glipizide and glyburide. Alcohol also lowers blood sugar by slowing the liver's glucose production. Together, the risk is higher, especially for people with diabetes, kidney problems, or who drink without eating. Watch for shakiness, sweating, confusion, and a racing heart.

**Does alcohol make Bactrim less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't chemically switch off the antibiotic, and there's no good evidence a single drink reduces how well it works. But drinking can lead to missed doses, vomiting up a dose, poorer sleep, and a weaker immune response, all of which can slow recovery. For a UTI, alcohol can also irritate the bladder and make symptoms feel worse.

**I drank one beer on Bactrim. Should I be worried?**

For a healthy adult, one beer is very unlikely to cause harm. Keep taking your antibiotic on schedule, drink some water, eat something, and avoid more alcohol until the course is finished. Contact a doctor if you notice flushing with a pounding heart, a new rash, severe nausea, or symptoms of low blood sugar.

**Is it safe to take DHM while on Bactrim?**

There's no good research on combining DHM with Bactrim, so it's best to wait until you've finished the course, or check with a pharmacist first. DHM does not make it safe to drink alcohol on an antibiotic, and there's no good evidence that it prevents a disulfiram-like reaction.
